claims.text: The FeNiCrCoCu coating is initially FCC.
The initial FeNiCrCoCu/Cu system has a low dislocation density.
Above 900 K, the system transitions from dislocation-mediated plasticity to localized amorphization and HCP nucleation.
Rapid dislocation annihilation above 900 K produces dislocation starvation.
Dislocation starvation reduces the ability of the coating to accommodate stress through slip.
At temperatures above 900 K, thermal energy overcomes the Peierls barrier and promotes dislocation climb.
The combination of high shear stress and thermal energy triggers a local FCC-to-HCP transformation.
Increasing temperature accelerates the FCC-to-HCP transformation observed at 77 K in CoCrFeMnNi.
The proposed HCP phase has lower stacking-fault energy.
Lattice-parameter differences associated with the transformed region hinder partial-dislocation motion.
The HCP phase has low shear strength and contributes to a low-viscosity interfacial layer.
Localized amorphization produces an unstable interfacial film that causes both a hardness drop and a friction-coefficient spike.
Above 900 K, the coefficient of friction increases while hardness and wear resistance decrease sharply.
HCP atom counting will show a localized peak in HCP fraction at the contact interface.
Total dislocation line length will decrease rapidly at high temperature relative to 600 K.
At 600 K, dislocation density is higher than at the proposed high-temperature starvation state.
At 600 K, increased elastic modulus and stable dislocation-mediated plasticity maintain wear resistance.
Finite-temperature local stacking-fault calculations slightly lower the FCC-HCP interfacial energy in CoCrFeMnNi over 300–900 K.
The mechanism may not apply to BCC HEAs because their dislocation behavior and phase stability differ from those of FCC HEAs.
An interfacial HCP fraction below 1% at high temperature would falsify HCP nucleation as the primary mediator.

contradictions.description: The HCP phase is assigned incompatible roles without reconciliation: it is described as a low-shear-strength constituent of a low-viscosity film, but also as a source of frictional resistance that hinders partial-dislocation motion.

The starvation hypothesis predicts that retaining or supplying dislocations should improve stress accommodation. The falsification rule initially treats worse performance of the pre-dislocated sample as contradictory to starvation, but then states that better performance of that sample indicates multiplication or entanglement rather than starvation. Better performance would instead be consistent with the proposed starvation mechanism.
